statement: Each of the $60$ members of a games club was asked which of chess, Go and checkers they enjoy. In total, $28$ members enjoy chess, $22$ enjoy Go and $20$ enjoy checkers. Also, $10$ enjoy both chess and Go, $8$ enjoy both chess and checkers, and $7$ enjoy both Go and checkers. These counts include the $3$ members who enjoy all three games. How many members enjoy exactly one of the three games?

choices.misconception: I found the number of members who enjoy none of the games, 60 - 48 = 12, instead of exactly one.
I found the members who enjoy exactly two of the games, 7 + 5 + 4 = 16, instead of exactly one.
I subtracted both pair counts from each game's total, but did not add back the 3 members who were subtracted twice: 10 + 5 + 5 = 20.
I found the 48 members who enjoy at least one game and subtracted all the pair counts, 48 - 25 = 23.

hints: Draw a Venn diagram with three circles and fill it in from the middle outward.
Put $3$ in the center. Then the 'chess and Go only' region has $10 - 3 = 7$, and so on for the other pairs.
Chess only is $28 - 7 - 5 - 3 = 13$. Find Go only and checkers only the same way and add.

solutions.reliable: Fill in a Venn diagram from the center. All three: $3$. Chess and Go only: $10 - 3 = 7$. Chess and checkers only: $8 - 3 = 5$. Go and checkers only: $7 - 3 = 4$. Then chess only is $28 - 7 - 5 - 3 = 13$, Go only is $22 - 7 - 4 - 3 = 8$ and checkers only is $20 - 5 - 4 - 3 = 8$. Exactly one game: $13 + 8 + 8 = 29$. Check: $29 + 16 + 3 = 48$ members enjoy at least one game, which matches $28 + 22 + 20 - 10 - 8 - 7 + 3 = 48$, leaving $12$ who enjoy none.
solutions.elegant: Let $E_1, E_2, E_3$ be the numbers enjoying exactly one, two and three games. Adding the three game totals counts these members $1, 2, 3$ times: $E_1 + 2E_2 + 3E_3 = 70$. Adding the three pair counts counts them $0, 1, 3$ times: $E_2 + 3E_3 = 25$. With $E_3 = 3$, $E_2 = 16$ and $E_1 = 70 - 32 - 9 = 29$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
